title: Government Doesn’t Need More Identity Silos. It Needs an Orchestration Strategy.
summary: Discover how biometric orchestration helps federal agencies reduce identity silos, improve security, and modernize identity verification systems.
body_markdown:
Federal agencies have invested heavily in technologies to establish, verify, and protect identity. From biometric matching and[liveness detection](https://www.aware.com/blog-liveness-detection-explained/) to document verification and digital authentication, these capabilities play an increasingly important role in national security, border protection, workforce access, and the delivery of citizen services.


But as identity technologies have expanded, so has the complexity of managing them.


Different agencies, departments, and programs often deploy identity systems to address specific operational needs. A border security program may rely on facial recognition to verify travelers, while a benefits agency uses remote identity proofing to prevent fraudulent enrollment. Another system may support biometric identification for law enforcement or secure access for government personnel.


Each investment may serve a legitimate purpose. The challenge emerges when these technologies operate independently, with different vendors, workflows, policies, and limited visibility across the broader identity environment.


> The result is a growing collection of identity capabilities without a cohesive strategy for managing them.


For federal leaders tasked with modernizing infrastructure, strengthening security, and making limited resources go further, adding another point solution isn’t necessarily the answer. What’s needed is a better way to connect, govern, and adapt the technologies already in place.


## The Hidden Costs of Fragmented Identity Infrastructure


Fragmentation isn’t unique to government, but the complexity of federal operations makes its consequences particularly significant. Agencies must support diverse missions, operate within strict regulatory and security requirements, and often maintain legacy systems that cannot be replaced overnight. Procurement cycles, evolving threats, and mission-specific technology requirements can further complicate modernization.


Over time, these conditions can create an environment where biometric capabilities are deployed independently rather than managed as part of a coordinated identity architecture. This introduces challenges that extend beyond integration costs.


When verification technologies operate in silos, it becomes harder to establish consistent security policies, evaluate performance across systems, or quickly introduce new capabilities. Agencies may also become dependent on individual vendors, limiting their ability to respond when an algorithm underperforms or new threats emerge.


Consider a government program that relies on facial recognition for remote identity verification. If fraudsters begin using more sophisticated deepfakes or injection attacks, the agency may need to introduce stronger liveness detection or additional risk signals. Within a rigid architecture, making that change could require substantial development, testing, and procurement effort.


The same challenge applies to operational performance. Without centralized visibility, agencies may struggle to understand where verification failures occur, which technologies are delivering the best results, or where unnecessary friction is slowing legitimate users.


> Fragmentation doesn’t just make identity systems harder to manage. It can make them slower to improve.


## From Point Solutions to Biometric Orchestration


[Biometric orchestration](https://www.aware.com/blog-biometric-orchestration-modern-identity-security/) offers a different approach.


Rather than treating individual biometric technologies as isolated components, biometric orchestration provides a common control layer for managing how they interact within identity verification workflows.


This can include technologies such as facial recognition, fingerprint matching, liveness detection, document verification, and other identity or risk signals. Through orchestration, agencies can determine which capabilities are used, under what conditions, and how their results contribute to an identity decision. Importantly, biometric orchestration is more than connecting systems through APIs. It is about creating a manageable environment where workflows, policies, and technology choices can be adjusted as operational needs change. For federal agencies, this approach introduces several important advantages.


### Greater Visibility and Consistent Governance


A shared orchestration layer can give agency leaders better visibility into how biometric technologies perform across supported workflows, including verification outcomes, failure patterns, processing times, and other operational metrics. It also provides an opportunity to manage identity policies more consistently rather than maintaining separate configurations across disconnected systems.


This doesn’t require every government program to use identical security measures. Different missions will always have different requirements. Instead, orchestration can establish common governance and oversight while allowing individual programs to maintain appropriate controls.


### Flexibility Without Vendor Dependency


No single biometric algorithm or provider will perform best in every environment or use case. A technology suited to high-volume airport identity verification may not be the optimal choice for remote citizen enrollment or large-scale biometric identification.


Orchestration gives agencies greater flexibility to select and combine technologies based on mission requirements, evaluate alternatives, and introduce new capabilities without redesigning entire identity systems. That flexibility becomes particularly valuable as biometric technologies advance and attack methods evolve.


### Risk-Based Identity Decisions


Not every identity interaction carries the same level of risk. A routine identity check may require a different verification process than a high-risk benefits transaction, sensitive account recovery, or access to a restricted government system.


Through orchestration, agencies can design workflows that adapt based on available risk signals and required assurance levels. Lower-risk interactions may proceed through streamlined verification, while higher-risk scenarios can trigger additional biometric checks, liveness detection, or human review. The objective is to apply appropriate security where it’s needed, without unnecessarily burdening every legitimate user.


## A More Practical Path to Federal Identity Modernization


Perhaps the most important advantage of orchestration is that modernization doesn’t always have to begin with replacing existing technology.


For agencies operating mission-critical systems, wholesale infrastructure changes can be expensive, time-consuming, and operationally disruptive. An orchestration strategy can support incremental modernization by connecting existing capabilities where technically feasible and introducing new technologies as requirements evolve.


This approach is already reflected in how agencies are planning future investments. U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) is[preparing to compete an application development contract worth up to $50 million](https://www.biometricupdate.com/202610/cbp-plans-up-to-50m-contract-for-biometrics-ai-integration) that could integrate biometric technology into both new and existing applications across the agency, alongside AI, data analytics, and mobile capabilities. As agencies pursue initiatives like this, an orchestration strategy can help ensure that new biometric capabilities strengthen a coordinated identity architecture rather than becoming another standalone system.


This approach also aligns with the broader direction of federal digital identity guidance. NIST SP 800-63-4 emphasizes risk management, identity assurance, fraud prevention, and the ongoing evaluation of digital identity systems. Orchestration is not itself a substitute for meeting these requirements, but it can provide an architectural foundation for implementing and managing relevant controls across complex identity environments.


Successful modernization also requires clear data governance, privacy protections, interoperability standards, and accountability for identity decisions. A common orchestration layer should strengthen these practices, not become another silo.


## Modernization is About More Than Technology


Federal agencies will continue to face pressure to improve services, reduce fraud, strengthen national security, and operate efficiently with constrained resources.


Meeting those expectations will require more than purchasing increasingly sophisticated biometric technologies. It will require the ability to manage those technologies as part of a coordinated strategy, one that provides visibility into performance, consistency in policy application, and flexibility to adapt without repeatedly rebuilding infrastructure.


The question for government leaders is no longer simply which biometric technology to deploy next. It’s whether their identity architecture allows them to use the technologies they have effectively, introduce better ones when needed, and make confident decisions across increasingly complex missions.


> The future of government identity security
>
>
> won’t
>
>
> be defined by how many systems agencies deploy, but by how intelligently those systems work together.
